name: Mozambique
summary: Cuban rhythm created by Pello el Afrokan (Pedro Izquierdo) in 1963 from the carnival comparsa: congas, bombos, cowbells and trombones, in rumba clave. Eddie Palmieri's New York mozambique (1965) took the name and the comparsa roots but no parts, and is in son clave; its bell is the one drumset players took up, most famously Steve Gadd.

hallmarks: a two-tone bell part phrased to the clave
the New York version: son clave, 2-3, and a different bell

archetype_patterns.name: Cuban mozambique bell over rumba clave, 2-3

evidence.note: Wikipedia's figure and MIDI file, from Changuito and Silverman (1998) p. 70. The file splits the bell into a low ('Bongo Bell') and a high ('Cha-cha bell') part; the figure writes them as two tones.

archetype_patterns.name: New York mozambique bell over son clave, 2-3
archetype_patterns.function: the bell drumset players play with the right hand

evidence.note: Wikipedia's 'NY-style Mozambique bell pattern in 2-3 clave'; son clave in 2-3 on Palmieri's records (Wikipedia; Bishop 2015, 2018). The bombo on the 'and' of 2 of the second bar always, of the first often (Bishop).

Tempo in half notes, from machine estimates (Deezer) of Pello el Afrokan's 'Mozambique' (116.5) and 'María Caracoles' (126.4) and Late in the Evening (118.5); no measured tempo was found. The New York mozambique is described here rather than given its own style; a separate style:new-york-mozambique would be more exact.
